name: Live Formative Checks
title: Live Formative Checks
answer: A live formative check is a quick question asked during a lesson, on a mini whiteboard or in a short online poll, that shows a teacher whether students understand before the class moves on. Its value comes from what the teacher does with the answers, since reteaching or working with a few students right away is what makes the check worth the class time. It matters because it gives teaching information in the moment rather than a score after the fact.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: The idea is that the most useful assessment often happens while a lesson is still running, not at the end of a unit. A teacher asks a quick question, students answer on a mini whiteboard or in a short online poll, and tools such as Google Forms collect the answers in seconds. AI can then group the responses so the teacher sees patterns at a glance instead of reading each one. The problem it solves is the gap between teaching and finding out whether the teaching landed, which otherwise stays hidden until a test or a graded assignment. A check that is gathered but never acted on is wasted class time.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom the routine is short and repeated: pose a question, collect answers quickly, and read the pattern. If most students missed the question, the teacher reteaches it right away. If only a few missed it, the teacher works with those students while the rest move ahead. The text does not describe separate versions of this routine for different grade bands, so the same cycle of asking, collecting, and responding applies across year groups. The technology covers only the collection step, since the teaching decision that follows stays with the teacher.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure, or evidence label for live formative checks, so this idea rests on practice rather than research as the book presents it. What the book states is a claim drawn from experience: that the most useful assessment often happens during a lesson, and that a check collected and never acted on is wasted class time. It also states that students who trust the process are more honest about their confusion. No numbers or named studies are given to support these claims.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Live checks should stay low stakes, so students feel free to show what they do not understand without fear of a grade. The purpose is information for teaching, not a score for the gradebook, and turning a check into a grade works against the honesty the process depends on. The decisions stay with the teacher: whether to reteach the whole class, work with a few students while others continue, or move on. AI only groups the responses so patterns are easier to see, and it does not decide what the teaching response should be. A check that is collected and then ignored is wasted class time, which is the main risk the text names.
